deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a fair copy of notes on ancient history: the Seleucid kings of Syria, continuing directly from the previous page and into the next. In order, the page says the following.

(1) Antiochus, brother of Seleucus IV and formerly a hostage at Rome, got help from Attalus of Pergamon and took the throne as Antiochus IV Epiphanes, dated '176–164'.

(2) He had grown used to Roman customs and wanted to keep them in Asia.

(3) He fought a successful war, dated '172–168', against Ptolemy VI Philometor, who had renewed claims on Syria (in the ancient sources, Coele-Syria). Antiochus invaded Egypt and took most of it. Philometor fled and fell into the Syrian king's hands. The Egyptians (Alexandrians) then put his brother Physcon (Ptolemy VIII) on the throne.

(4) In 169 Antiochus besieged Alexandria again. Rome sent an embassy ordering him to leave Egypt at once. He did so, returned what he had taken, and took Philometor with him.

(5) In 165 Antiochus led an expedition to Upper Asia to enrich himself and died on the way.

(6) Antiochus V Eupator, dated '164–161', stood under a guardianship; the sentence continues on the next page with Lysias and Philip.

The page contains no derivations, formulas or numbers other than regnal and event dates. Nothing in it can be reconstructed mathematically. The hand and content look like lecture notes or a student's copy on ancient history, filed in this bundle.
errors: Antiochus IV Epiphanes came to the throne in 175 BC, not 176. Seleucus IV was murdered by Heliodorus in 175.
The Sixth Syrian War is usually dated 170–168 BC, not 172–168.

The Roman ultimatum is wrongly dated. The embassy of C. Popillius Laenas (the 'Day of Eleusis', the circle drawn in the sand) came in 168 BC, during Antiochus' second invasion. The second siege of Alexandria belongs to 168, not 169.

The claim that Antiochus 'took Philometor with him' is doubtful. In 169 he left Philometor at Memphis as a rival king to Physcon. By 168 the two Ptolemies had reconciled and ruled jointly, so Antiochus did not carry Philometor off to Syria.
Antiochus IV died late in 164 BC at Tabae in Persis, during the eastern campaign that began in 165. That is consistent with the page, apart from the dating.

Antiochus V Eupator reigned 164–162 BC; Demetrius I had him killed in 162. The page's '164–161' (and the next page's Demetrius I '161–150') is a year off from the usual chronology of 162–150 for Demetrius I.
Physcon was proclaimed king in Alexandria around 170/169. The page's ordering of events compresses the sequence.

results.what: Historical narrative of the Seleucid succession and the Sixth Syrian War (Antiochus IV vs. Ptolemy VI/VIII, Roman intervention)
results.modern_name: Hellenistic history: Seleucid chronology / Sixth Syrian War
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient sources (Polybius, Livy, Diodorus, Justin, Appian); a standard 18th/19th-century textbook narrative

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds routine history notes on the Seleucids, of the kind found in early-19th-century lectures or compendia. It contains no mathematics and nothing original, and it may not even be in Gauss's own hand.

checkable.asserts: Under the standard chronology (175–164 BC), Antiochus IV reigned about 11 years. The page's 176–164 gives 12.
Under the standard chronology, Antiochus V Eupator reigned about 2 years. The page's 164–161 gives 3.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: the image appears to read 'setzte sich auf' rather than 'setzt sich auf'.
Line 2: 'den Thron' (the image has 'den Throne', i.e. 'dem Throne'/'den Thron').
Line 15: the insertion 'nach' is written above the line, replacing a struck 'nach'. The destination is 'Ober-Asien' (Upper Asia), with an 'a' struck and rewritten.
Line 16: 'Er starb auf der Reise' is written in heavily abbreviated form ('Er st[ar]b a[uf] d[er] Reise'). The reading is plausible.
Line 8: 'Philometor wurde verjagt' is correct, as is 'fiel dem syrischen König in die Hände'. 'Größten-theils' should be read as 'des größten Theils'.
